node.label: Ellen Ross
node.date_label: Sex and Society, with Rayna Rapp (1981) · “Fierce Questions and Taunts” (1982) · Survival Networks (1983) · Love and Toil (1993) · Slum Travelers, editor (2007)
node.description: In Love and Toil: Motherhood in Outcast London, 1870–1918 (1993), Ellen Ross argued that mothers’ domestic choices were essential to the survival and cultural continuity of the British working classes. The book makes poor London mothers’ distinctive experience central to working-class history. Carolyn Steedman’s 1994 review situated it within research on women’s reproduction of everyday life and highlighted its dependence on earlier women investigators’ records. Emma Griffin’s 2018 study of maternal emotions challenged Ross and other historians for finding maternal love in autobiographical accounts that also described emotional distance and violence. Ross’s Slum Travelers (2007), an edited and annotated anthology with an introduction, recovered women’s investigations of London poverty and their representations of the urban poor.
node.representative_figures_and_works: With Rayna Rapp, “Sex and Society: A Research Note from Social History and Anthropology” (1981; republished 1983); “Survival Networks” (1983); Love and Toil: Motherhood in Outcast London, 1870–1918 (1993); with Judith R. Walkowitz, “Raphael Samuel (1934–1996): An Appreciation” (1997); editor, Slum Travelers: Ladies and London Poverty, 1860–1920 (2007).
node.scope_note: Books and the 1997 appreciation were not read in full. Love and Toil was assessed through its publisher abstract, Steedman’s first-page review preview and selected passages of Griffin’s accepted manuscript. Slum Travelers acknowledgments were read only as a substantial indexed publisher extract; direct access failed. For the 1981 coauthored article, only the opening extract and displayed notes were read. Survival Networks is known here through bibliographic metadata.

proposed_edges.relationship: In “Sex and Society” (1981), Ross and Rayna Rapp explicitly adopt Foucault’s historical account of what counts as sexual.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Cambridge Core, displayed note 2: “We agree with Foucault’s contention.” Explicit joint attribution, not a claim about Ross alone. The note cites the 1978 English translation of The History of Sexuality, volume 1 (French original 1976); opening and notes read, complete article and Foucault volume unread.

proposed_edges.evidence_note: Walkowitz institutional CV, p. 3, publication beginning With Ellen Ross. Authorship and year only; appreciation unread. This undirected collaboration differs from Walkowitz’s contribution to the 2007 introduction.

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 2020 review of Emma Griffin’s Bread Winner, Jane Humphries drew upon Ellen Ross’s Love and Toil: Motherhood in Outcast London, 1870–1918 (1993) as an earlier study using autobiography to explain working-class motherhood, in arguing that Griffin needed to engage with preceding research on families and deprivation.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the journal’s print version of Humphries’s review. Humphries identifies Ross’s method and substantive achievement in the body of her argument about insufficient engagement with earlier research; this is more than a bibliography entry or a list of names. The claim is limited to Humphries’s use of Ross as a historiographical precedent in this review. It does not establish formative influence on Humphries’s earlier books. Jane Humphries is present in the supplied run-members list and therefore carries pending_endpoint: true. Neither Ross’s book nor Griffin’s book was read in full for this task.
proposed_edges.map_label: Earlier study used to assess Bread Winner, 2020

proposed_edges.relationship: Ellen Ross’s Love and Toil: Motherhood in Outcast London, 1870–1918 (1993) contributed to the history of motherhood by analysing class tensions between working-class mothers and women working in infant welfare organizations, an argument identified by Anna Muggeridge and Ruth Davidson in their 2026 historiographical review.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Read the publisher’s open article introduction and its discussion of maternalism, including the named argument and footnote 8. The authors attribute the argument jointly to Dyhouse, Lewis, and Ross; the edge does not claim Ross originated it alone. The demography endpoint explicitly includes the history of the family and intimate relations. This proposal concerns motherhood and maternal welfare within that scope, not demographic measurement or family reconstitution. The text substantively explains Ross’s argument in the body rather than merely listing a citation. No claim of having read Love and Toil in full is made.
proposed_edges.map_label: Class tensions in histories of motherhood, 1993

proposed_edges.relationship: In her 1994 Albion review, Steedman placed Love and Toil (1993) within research on women's reproduction of everyday life and noted its dependence on earlier women investigators' records.
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Albion 26:3 (1994), pp. 550–551, first page read on Cambridge Core at verification. A published review engaging the argument; added from Fable's review (F09-015).
